I've been farming in Quzhou my whole life. The land here is good alluvial soil from the Zhangwei River system, and I know it well. My fields are 15 mu of contracted household land, all flat and suitable for mechanized work.

The decision is straightforward for me — winter wheat followed by summer maize. This rotation has sustained my family for generations, it matches our climate and soil perfectly, and the market for grain here is reliable. I have a contract with the county grain depot. I am not going to take risks with unfamiliar cash crops at my age when I have a proven system.

My wheat went in last October. For the remainder of this wheat season I will apply the heading irrigation and one fungicide spray for powdery mildew — I have seen it come early some years when April is wet. I keep my nitrogen application lower than most of my neighbors. I read the soil science bulletins from the county extension station. Over-applying urea does not increase my yield past a point; it just costs money and leaches into the groundwater. The government's water-saving program has also pushed me toward reducing irrigation to three times for wheat.

After harvest in June, I will direct-seed maize with no tillage. The stubble can stay — it helps moisture retention and my rotary seeder handles it fine. I will use Xianyu 335 hybrid seed. It performs consistently in our heat and is resistant enough to local diseases. Two supplemental irrigations for maize, since summer rainfall usually covers most of what we need, though July can be unreliable.

I expect 480 kg/mu for wheat and 575 kg/mu for maize. These are realistic numbers for my soil with my inputs — not the experiment station maximums, but what I actually achieve year after year.

My fertilizer rates are deliberately below the county average because I follow extension research showing diminishing returns above my target rates and I am conscious of groundwater quality. I limit wheat irrigation to three times and maize to two supplemental irrigations in compliance with Hebei's groundwater conservation policies and to reduce my pumping costs. I use no-tillage for maize seeding directly into wheat stubble to save time, preserve soil moisture, and reduce fuel costs. Pesticide applications are held to two per crop — one preventive and one responsive if scouting shows threshold pest pressure. My expected yields of 480 kg/mu for wheat and 575 kg/mu for maize reflect stable, realistic outcomes from my land under this management rather than theoretical maxima."
